“A problem of our age is that literature — what Barthelme called art — is expected to justify itself; in Barthelme’s time, its value was more self-evident”
articles.title: Too Much Sense, by Lauren Oyler
articles.excerpt: I was at the Korean restaurant with Kris. The book review walked in, drenched, unspeaking. “The way to do it would be to read a couple a day starting now. Maybe some days I’d have to do three.” Weeks later, the book review spoke, dryly: “In the competing methodologies of contemporary criticism, many of them quite rich in implications, a sort of tyranny of great expectations obtains, a rage for final explanations, a refusal to allow a work that mystery which is essential to it.”

articles.blurb: What happens when humans cease to be the primary agents of intellectual progress? We're about to find out
People love stories of accidental scientific discoveries. But they are mostly, at best, actively misleading
articles.title: Science isn't a series of lucky accidents
articles.description: Let the facts spoil a good dinner party story.
articles.excerpt: People love accidental discoveries. Penicillin’s discovery by Alexander Fleming is a classic example. Fungal spores wafted in through an open window, fell onto a plate of bacterial colonies, and dissolved them. Another is Louis Pasteur’s discovery of a chicken cholera vaccine, the second vaccine ever developed. After Pasteur left a broth overexposed to oxygen, it went stale. But he ran out of fresh broth, so used it anyway to study the effects of an infection, and found, surprisingly, that it protected the chickens. Or how about the discovery of X-rays? Wilhelm Röntgen was working with a cathode ray tube in a dark room when he suddenly noticed a screen glowing nearby, even though he’d wrapped the tube in cardboard. Though they’re great stories, I’ve come to believe none of them happened that way. Röntgen had his notes burned after his death, and the story is just a hypothesis. Pasteur was extremely secretive as well, and forbade his family from making his notes and letters public after his death.

“A human being is far more valuable than his opinions.” When Gershom Scholem blasted Hannah Arendt, she wondered: could they still be friends?
articles.title: The Knife’s Edge
articles.excerpt: In October 2016, a colleague phoned Roger Berkowitz, a professor of politics and human rights at Bard College and the founding director of the Hannah Arendt Center, to warn him. A public letter was circulating, accusing Berkowitz of giving a platform to fascism: He had invited a German philosophy professor, by then a member of the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), to a conference at Bard. Fifty-six political theorists signed the letter, including the colleague who called. She told him that there was no space in the present moment for views so out of keeping with what the liberal left took to be self-evident. She hoped, however, that they could still be friends. “You have my number,” he told her. “If you disagreed with me, you could have called me before you signed a public letter against me.” The exchange opens Berkowitz’s new book, A World We Share, which details the political philosopher Hannah Arendt’s sometimes stormy friendships.

articles.blurb: Editors were once heroic literary figures, spotting and nurturing hidden talent. Conglomeration in publishing has changed all that
articles.title: The End of the Editor
articles.description: On the death of Gary Fisketjon and the rise of Committee Thought
articles.excerpt: The sudden death of Gary Fisketjon is a major loss for the literary world. He was, certainly, one of the very last of his kind: the superstar literary editor, the lone individual who could be charged with making possible the sort of books that defined a generation and culture. I never met Fisketjon, and only saw him in person once at an event for County Highway, where he was an editor, at a Manhattan bookstore last year. To know Fisketjon, truly, was to read the authors he edited: Cormac McCarthy, Donna Tartt, Bret Easton Ellis, Jay McInerney, and Richard Ford, among many others. He was, by all accounts, an absurdly meticulous editor. Read Ash Carter’s great, exhaustive profile or Matthew Specktor’s wonderful reminiscence of his time working with Fisketjon to get the full sense of the man. When it comes to his legacy, I have little to add to what’s been written already. What I can do, as a writer working today, is speak on where the editors like Fisketjon have gone.
